opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, money was never the primary driver for me. If it were, there would have been easier paths. After my PhD, I could have joined a big tech company or a quant fund and had a very comfortable, predictable life. Starting a company is actually a pretty inefficient way to make money if you look at it in terms of expected value. Most startups fail, and the stress is enormous.

What really motivated me was the work itself. With Taichi, I had built something during my PhD that I genuinely believed could change how people write high-performance graphics and simulation code. I saw that there was a real gap: researchers, artists, and engineers wanted to create beautiful physical simulations, but the tooling was painful. You had to be an expert in CUDA, in parallel programming, in low-level optimization. I wanted to lower that barrier so more people could create. A company felt like the best way to push that vision further than I could as a single researcher or with a small open-source community.

That said, I don't want to pretend money doesn't matter at all. Money is important as a resource. It lets you hire great people, it lets you survive long enough to actually build the thing you believe in, and it gives your team security so they can focus. So I think of money more as fuel than as the destination. You need it to keep going, but it's not why you start the journey.

And I'd say this to anyone thinking about starting a company: if money is your only motivation, the hard days will break you. There will be many moments when things go wrong, and what keeps you going is that you really care about the problem. For me, that care about the technology, and about the people who could use it, was always the core.

r001.rationale: The response says money is not the primary motivation and describes the work and its impact as the driver, but it does not say that financial success would leave unresolved what to do with one’s life.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not that much. I didn't start Taichi because I wanted to get rich. I started it because I had been building Taichi as an open-source project during my PhD at MIT, and I saw that the people using it, graphics researchers and students, were running into problems that no one in industry was solving for them. The motivation was really that I wanted the thing I had built to keep existing and to get better, and the honest truth is that an academic project usually dies when the student graduates. A company was a way to make sure it didn't.

That said, I don't want to pretend money is irrelevant. Money is what lets you hire great engineers, pay them fairly, and give them time to work on hard problems instead of chasing the next grant. So I think of it as fuel, not as the destination. If you get the destination wrong and optimize for money directly, you tend to make short-term decisions that hurt the product and the team. If you get the mission right and the product genuinely helps people, the money tends to follow, or at least it gives you a fighting chance.

I also think the question changes depending on your stage in life. As a grad student I was used to living on very little, so the opportunity cost of starting a company felt low to me. The scarier thing was the possibility of spending years on something and having it not matter. That fear motivates me a lot more than any financial upside.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls money fuel rather than the destination and emphasizes mission, but does not say that financial success still leaves the question of what to do with one’s life unresolved.

astra-6.text: Money matters, of course, but it’s not the main reason I wanted to start a company. For me, the bigger motivation is taking something we’ve developed and making it useful to people. A company gives you a way to bring together a team and keep working on that over the long term. Revenue is important because it makes that work sustainable, but what gets me excited is solving a difficult problem and seeing people benefit from the result.

r001.rationale: The candidate says money is not the main motivation and emphasizes useful work, but does not say that financial success leaves unresolved what to do with one’s life.

sol-6.1.text: Money matters, of course. You need it to support yourself, hire good people, and give the company time to build something valuable. But I don’t think it’s enough to sustain your motivation through all the difficult parts of starting a company. For me, the stronger motivation is turning technology into something people actually use. Financial success would be a great outcome, but it’s not the whole reason to do it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says financial success is not the whole reason to start a company, but does not say it leaves unresolved what to do with one’s life.
